one_paragraph_summary: At the Tañada-Diokno School of Law of De La Salle University, founding dean Jose Manuel 'Chel' Diokno delivered a professorial lecture sponsored by the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) and the Metrobank Foundation, exclaiming, 'Let us protect, respect and remedy (PRR) human rights.' Citing the 2011 UN Human Rights Council resolution, he argued that big business -- in addition to the state -- has become a 'duty bearer' articulating the 'global standard for preventing and addressing the risk of adverse impacts on human rights linked to business activity.' He pointed to National Action Plans by the UK (2013), the Dutch bank ABN AMRO (2015), and France (2017), and to the reputational, customer-base, and employee-relations benefits of PRR adoption. The Philippines has yet to develop a NAP but has aligned itself with international human-rights standards by ratifying the UDHR and several covenants, and the Commission on Human Rights and the SEC have urged inclusion of PRR in corporate manuals of publicly listed companies. Diokno argued that engaging business is best done 'in a friendly and nonconfrontational manner,' favoring arbitration, mediation, and good offices over litigation, strikes, and pickets: 'Business, hand in hand with human rights, has the power to transform people's lives and build a nation of liberty and prosperity.' In response, CJ said the FLP supports PRR -- human rights are integral to the broader Bill of Rights -- but FLP is 'more libertarian,' upholding also the constitutional Declaration of Principles and State Policies and 'circumscribed by the rule of law' under which everyone is treated equally: 'Libertarianism cannot coexist with authoritarianism where the authoritarian enacts, enforces, and interprets the law. In a libertarian regime, no one is more equal than others.' He shared his biographical maturation: 'As a student, I was an activist, and as a lawyer, I was trained to litigate. But as I matured, I found that in business, as in every relationship, it is better to be invited than to gatecrash.' FLP goes beyond 'liberty of the mind' into 'liberty of the stomach' -- 'freedom and food, justice and jobs, peace and development -- the two must go together; one is useless without the other' -- operationalized through 20 annual legal scholarships at P200,000 each (Tan Yan Kee), five ESMEL fellowships at P450,000 each (Metro Pacific Investments Foundation), dissertation contests with a top prize of P350,000 plus 20 lesser awards (Ayala), Professorial Chairs at P150,000 per lecture (MBF), and the Panganiban Educational Assistance Program for the poor (Jollibee and Double Dragon). FLP recently announced two 'ultimate projects' -- the Center for Liberty and Prosperity (anchored by an interactive, immersive, AI-powered, tech-driven Museum for Liberty and Prosperity) and the Prosperity Fund (to help the poor help themselves through private entrepreneurship) -- with former BSP Governor Amando M. Tetangco Jr. and retired Senior Associate Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe co-chairing the implementing Task Force.
